\chapter{The Land}
\label{ch:ta-the-land}
\hlchaptermodality{53}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a river, a hill, a paddy field, a path and a village in Tamil.}

Complete TA-C53-village and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nadi]{\ta{நதி} (nadi) — a river}

\label{lesson:TA-C53-river}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{vēr} mean, and what did \emph{vitai} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{நதி}}
\textbf{\ta{நதி}} (\emph{nadi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a river\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{nadī}, and Telugu prints it identically: \te{నది}. Malayalam did not take it for the everyday river and says \ml{പുഴ} (\emph{puḻa}) instead, which is its own.

Tamil's inherited river is \ta{ஆறு} — the same shape as the six you already count with. Which of the two is meant comes out of what sits around it, and \ta{நதி} is the one that leaves no room for doubt.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things in a stretch of country.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nadi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vitai}, then \emph{nadi}, the seed and the water that reaches it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{நதி} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a river\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[malai]{\ta{மலை} (malai) — a hill}

\label{lesson:TA-C53-hill}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nadi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மலை}}
\textbf{\ta{மலை}} (\emph{malai}) — \textquotedblleft{}a hill\textquotedblright{}.

Proto-Dravidian, and it covers a hill and a mountain both — Tamil does not split them the way English does. Telugu keeps a small hill of its own, \te{గుట్ట} (\emph{guṭṭa}).

You have been reading this word all along without being told. The name \emph{Malayāḷam} begins with it: the language of the hill country, named for its hills.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: the water, and what it comes down from.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{malai}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nadi}, then \emph{malai}, the water and the high ground behind it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மலை} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a hill\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vayal]{\ta{வயல்} (vayal) — a paddy field}

\label{lesson:TA-C53-field}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{malai} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{வயல்}}
\textbf{\ta{வயல்}} (\emph{vayal}) — \textquotedblleft{}a paddy field\textquotedblright{}.

A wet field: the flooded one that grows rice, not a dry one. Malayalam writes \ml{വയൽ} and means the same thing by it.

The dry field is a \emph{kollai}, a different word altogether, and the split earns its keep. A farmer telling you which of the two he has is telling you what he can grow on it and when.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: high ground, and now the flat wet ground under it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vayal}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{malai}, then \emph{vayal}, the high ground and the flat
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{வயல்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a paddy field\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pātai]{\ta{பாதை} (pātai) — a path}

\label{lesson:TA-C53-path}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vayal} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{பாதை}}
\textbf{\ta{பாதை}} (\emph{pātai}) — \textquotedblleft{}a path\textquotedblright{}.

Something you can put your foot on: a track worn into the ground, a lane, a road.

Tamil has \emph{vaḻi} as well, and the two overlap less than they look as though they should. \emph{vaḻi} is the way — the route, the means, the manner of going about something. \ta{பாதை} stays physical. Malayalam's everyday path-word is \ml{വഴി}, the same one; Telugu's is \emph{bāṭa}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four: three places, and now something joining them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pātai}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vayal}, then \emph{pātai}, the field and the way to it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{பாதை} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a path\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kirāmam]{\ta{கிராமம்} (kirāmam) — a village}

\label{lesson:TA-C53-village}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pātai} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{கிராமம்}}
\textbf{\ta{கிராமம்}} (\emph{kirāmam}) — \textquotedblleft{}a village\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{grāma}, and Telugu takes it whole: \te{గ్రామం}. Tamil does not begin a word on two held-together sounds, so it let a vowel into the middle of the cluster and the word came out \emph{ki-rā-mam}.

You already have \emph{ūr} for the place you belong to. \emph{ūr} is yours — your town, the one you name when somebody asks where you are from. \ta{கிராமம்} is the word on the form and on the signboard at the edge of the road.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Water, high ground, a wet field, a way across it, and the place at the end of the way.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kirāmam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{nadi}, \emph{malai}, \emph{vayal}, \emph{pātai}, \emph{kirāmam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{கிராமம்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a village\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
